newsitem.title: USA: Shapiro explains 'fast-track' trade to US governors.
newsitem.headline: Shapiro explains 'fast-track' trade to US governors.

text.p: Senior U.S. trade negotiator Ira Shapiro warned on Sunday of lost markets and opportunity if Congress fails to give President Bill Clinton "fast-track" authority in trade negotiations.
Shapiro told the nation's governors winning "fast-track" authority was a top priority, but securing congressional approval would not be easy and could take time.
Under the "fast-track" authority sought by the White House, Congress would be required to vote within 60 days, and without amendment, on trade deals negotiated before June 1, 2003.
Although others have filed more restrictive "fast-track" bills than the White House desires, the Clinton administration has yet to send a "fast-track" proposal to Congress.
"None of us are underestimating the difficulty of the work ahead in pursuing 'fast track'," Shapiro told the winter meeting of the National Governors Association.

"Many in Congress opposed some of our earlier trade agreements, and there are many who object to the notion of 'fast track' as some kind of encroachment on the role of the legislative process," he said.

At the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, House Speaker Newt Gingrich said he favoured "fast-track" authority for Clinton, and said he did not see a problem getting agreement from Republican House members.
But Gingrich said approval of the measure could face congressional hurdles if the Clinton administration insisted on "dumping all sorts of social policies" into trade pacts.
Shapiro refused to predict when an administration proposal would be filed, saying a bipartisan consensus needed to be explored first.
Shapiro said the United States risks ceding business, particularly in Latin America, to other countries if Congress refused to give Clinton "fast-track" authority.
"The ability to work this out and forge a new bipartisan consensus, in our view, is fundamental to our ability to compete successfully in the most dynamic areas of the world," Shapiro said.

He singled out Latin America as an international trade region being targeted aggressively by U.S. competitors. American exports to Latin America are expected to exceed all of the exports to Europe and Japan combined by 2010.
"We need to be reasserting our leadership in Latin America, pursuing a free trade area of the Americas starting with Chile, where our lack of 'fast-track' authority has hurt," Shapiro said.
